meta.connection: On the mat you can name your own mistake in a round without blaming your partner. Owning your part of a rupture works the same way. It starts with separating your piece from theirs.

slides.title: When something breaks, what part is yours to own?

body.text: This is a takedown to one leg, twice.

items: The attacker wins when the defender's hips or hands touch the mat.
The defender wins by freeing himself completely.

body.text: This is passing the legs from on top.

items: The top player wins by touching both of the bottom player's knee pits with his own leg, feet off the mat.
The bottom player wins by making the top player sit down, then sitting up himself.

body.text: This is separating hands to trap one arm.

items: The top player wins by separating the bottom player's hands and locking two grips on his wrist.
The bottom player wins by freeing his own trapped arm, or by reversing the position.

slides.title: What made it work?
slides.question: Tonight you built a position standing, passing, and pinning, and it was yours to hold or let go. What made it yours?

options.text: You owned both the hold and the release.
options.feedback: Owning your part means owning the release too, not just the win.

options.text: You owned it only while you were winning.
options.feedback: Only owning the winning part is not owning your whole part.

options.text: You owned it only once it was over.
options.feedback: Waiting until it's over to own it is too late.

body.text: Tonight you worked from a single leg, open guard, and an arm lock position. On the mat you can name your mistake without blaming your partner. Owning a break works the same way: separate your piece from theirs. You get to own your part and let the rest be his.
